claim: Rodent herpesvirus Peru (RHVP) encodes a Qa-1 like protein (pQa-1) via RNA splicing.
source: Here, we report that rodent herpesvirus Peru (RHVP) encodes a Qa-1 like protein (pQa-1) via RNA splicing to counteract NK activation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the discovery of pQa-1 and demonstrates through RT-PCR and sequencing that it is produced via RNA splicing.

claim: pQa-1 surface expression is stabilized by the same canonical peptides presented by murine Qa-1.
source: While pQa-1 surface expression is stabilized by the same canonical peptides presented by murine Qa-1, pQa-1 is GPI-anchored and resistant to the activity of RHVP pK3, a ubiquitin ligase that targets MHC-I for degradation.
evidence: The manuscript presents peptide-binding assays showing that pQa-1 surface levels are enhanced by Qdm and Qdm-like peptides.

claim: pQa-1 is GPI-anchored.
source: While pQa-1 surface expression is stabilized by the same canonical peptides presented by murine Qa-1, pQa-1 is GPI-anchored and resistant to the activity of RHVP pK3, a ubiquitin ligase that targets MHC-I for degradation.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates through PI-PLC treatment that pQa-1 is GPI-anchored.

claim: pQa-1 is resistant to the activity of RHVP pK3.
source: While pQa-1 surface expression is stabilized by the same canonical peptides presented by murine Qa-1, pQa-1 is GPI-anchored and resistant to the activity of RHVP pK3, a ubiquitin ligase that targets MHC-I for degradation.
evidence: The manuscript shows through flow cytometry that pQa-1 surface expression remains unchanged in the presence of pK3, unlike classical MHC-I and Qa-1.

claim: RHVP pK3 is a ubiquitin ligase that targets MHC-I for degradation.
source: While pQa-1 surface expression is stabilized by the same canonical peptides presented by murine Qa-1, pQa-1 is GPI-anchored and resistant to the activity of RHVP pK3, a ubiquitin ligase that targets MHC-I for degradation.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work and presents data showing pK3 downregulates MHC-I.

claim: pQa-1 tetramer staining indicates that it recognizes CD94/NKG2A receptors.
source: pQa-1 tetramer staining indicates that it recognizes CD94/NKG2A receptors.
evidence: The manuscript presents tetramer staining data showing pQa-1 binds to CD94/NKG2A+ cells.

claim: pQa-1 selectively inhibits NKG2A+ NK cells.
source: Consistently, pQa-1 selectively inhibits NKG2A+ NK cells and expression of pQa-1 can protect tumor cells from NK control in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript presents NK activation assays showing reduced IFNγ production and CD107a expression in NKG2A+ NK cells when cultured with pQa-1-expressing cells.

claim: Expression of pQa-1 can protect tumor cells from NK control in vivo.
source: Consistently, pQa-1 selectively inhibits NKG2A+ NK cells and expression of pQa-1 can protect tumor cells from NK control in vivo.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from a murine melanoma metastasis model showing increased lung metastases in mice challenged with pQa-1-expressing B16F10 cells.

claim: Herpesviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses.
source: Herpesviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses that are associated with malignancies and can persist in the presence of an active immune system in part through their ability to avoid detection by both cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) and NK cells (Odom et al., 2012; Feng et al., 2013; Noriega et al., 2012), two major branches of host cellular defense in adaptive and innate immunity, respectively.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about herpesviruses.

claim: Herpesviruses are associated with malignancies.
source: Herpesviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses that are associated with malignancies and can persist in the presence of an active immune system in part through their ability to avoid detection by both cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) and NK cells (Odom et al., 2012; Feng et al., 2013; Noriega et al., 2012), two major branches of host cellular defense in adaptive and innate immunity, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Herpesviruses can persist in the presence of an active immune system through their ability to avoid detection by CTL and NK cells.
source: Herpesviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses that are associated with malignancies and can persist in the presence of an active immune system in part through their ability to avoid detection by both cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) and NK cells (Odom et al., 2012; Feng et al., 2013; Noriega et al., 2012), two major branches of host cellular defense in adaptive and innate immunity, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CTL and NK cells are two major branches of host cellular defense in adaptive and innate immunity, respectively.
source: Herpesviruses are large double-stranded DNA viruses that are associated with malignancies and can persist in the presence of an active immune system in part through their ability to avoid detection by both cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL) and NK cells (Odom et al., 2012; Feng et al., 2013; Noriega et al., 2012), two major branches of host cellular defense in adaptive and innate immunity, respectively.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: CTL detect foreign antigens presented by MHC-I through TCR engagement with MHC-I/peptide complexes.
source: CTL detect foreign antigens presented by major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) by engagement of their TCR with MHC-I/peptide complexes on the surface of target cells.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge about CTL function.

claim: Numerous viral proteins disrupt MHC-I antigen presentation pathways.
source: The importance of CTL function in control of viral infection is highlighted by numerous examples of viral proteins disrupting MHC-I antigen presentation pathways (Hansen and Bouvier, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: NK cells can respond and kill viral infected cells rapidly without the need for priming and expansion.
source: In contrast to CTL, functional NK cells can respond and kill viral infected cells rapidly without the need for priming and expansion.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge about NK cell function.

claim: NK cells are vital in the control of herpesvirus infection.
source: NK cells are also vital in the control of herpesvirus infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent examples and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Individuals with selective NK cell deficiencies often exhibit recurrent and severe herpesvirus infections.
source: In humans, for example, individuals with selective NK cell deficiencies, either in number or function, often exhibit recurrent and severe herpesvirus infections including α−herpesviruses (VZV, HSV), β−herpesviruses (CMV) and γ−herpesviruses (EBV) (reviewed in (Orange, 2013)).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: NK cell-depletion confers susceptibility upon inbred strains of mice otherwise resistant to MCMV infection.
source: Similarly, NK cell-depletion confers susceptibility upon inbred strains of mice otherwise resistant to murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) infection (Scalzo et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: NK cell activity against viral-infected targets is balanced by integrated signals from inhibitory and activating receptors.
source: NK cell activity against viral-infected targets is balanced by integrated signals from inhibitory and activating receptors.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge about NK cell regulation.

claim: MHC-I molecules serve as ligands for NK cell inhibitory receptors.
source: In addition to presenting peptides that activate antigen-specific CTL, MHC-I molecules also serve as ligands for NK cell inhibitory receptors.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: Normal, ubiquitous expression of MHC-I protects healthy cells from NK killing.
source: The normal, ubiquitous expression of MHC-I protects healthy cells from NK killing.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge about the 'missing-self' hypothesis.

claim: When MHC-I antigen presentation is sabotaged by pathogens, NK cells are released from inhibition and may attack infected cells.
source: When MHC-I antigen presentation is sabotaged by pathogens, NK cells are released from inhibition and consequently may attack infected cells.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge about the 'missing-self' hypothesis.

claim: The loss of surface MHC-I is often referred to as 'missing-self'.
source: The loss of surface MHC-I is often referred to a 'missing-self' (Jensen et al., 2004; Yokoyama et al., 2010; Natarajan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many viruses have evolved strategies for coping with 'missing-self' attack by NK cells.
source: Not surprisingly, along with their CTL evasion mechanisms, many viruses have also evolved strategies for coping with 'missing-self' attack by NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent examples in the manuscript.

claim: One viral NK evasion strategy is the selective upregulation of surface expression of HLA-E in humans and Qa-1 in mice.
source: One such strategy is the selective upregulation of surface expression of HLA-E in humans and Qa-1 in mice, the non-classical MHC-I proteins that serve as ligands for the NK cell inhibitory receptor CD94/NKG2A.
evidence: This claim is supported by subsequent examples in the manuscript.

claim: HLA-E and Qa-1 are non-classical MHC-I proteins that serve as ligands for the NK cell inhibitory receptor CD94/NKG2A.
source: One such strategy is the selective upregulation of surface expression of HLA-E in humans and Qa-1 in mice, the non-classical MHC-I proteins that serve as ligands for the NK cell inhibitory receptor CD94/NKG2A.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: HCMV UL40 selectively stabilizes surface HLA-E by providing a nonameric peptide that is loaded on to HLA-E in the ER independent of TAP.
source: For example, UL40 encoded by human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) selectively stabilizes surface HLA-E by providing a nonameric peptide that is loaded on to HLA-E in the ER yet independent of transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP) (Tomasec et al., 2000; Ulbrecht et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HCMV US2, US11, KSHV kK5, and HIV nef induce profound downregulation of classical MHC-I but do not compromise HLA-E expression.
source: Other viral immune evasion proteins such as HCMV US2 and US11, Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) kK5, and HIV nef, induce profound downregulation of classical MHC-I but do not compromise HLA-E expression (Orange et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The CD94/NKG2 family of receptors are type-II transmembrane heterodimers that possess C-type lectin ectodomains.
source: The CD94/NKG2 family of receptors are type-II transmembrane heterodimers that possess C-type lectin ectodomains.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: CD94/NKG2 receptors are conserved in humans and mice and expressed on large percentages of NK cells.
source: They are conserved in humans and mice and expressed on large percentages of NK cells (Petrie et al., 2008; Hoare et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Each member of the CD94/NKG2 family comprises an invariant CD94 polypeptide disulfide linked to either NKG2A/B, -C, -E or -F.
source: Each member of this family comprises an invariant CD94 polypeptide disulfide linked to either NKG2A/B, -C, -E or -F.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: NKG2A and NKG2B are inhibitory NK receptors.
source: NKG2A and -B (a spliced form of –A) are inhibitory whereas NKG2C and -E are activating NK receptors (Kaiser et al., 2005; Braud et al., 1998b; Lazetic et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NKG2C and NKG2E are activating NK receptors.
source: NKG2A and -B (a spliced form of –A) are inhibitory whereas NKG2C and -E are activating NK receptors (Kaiser et al., 2005; Braud et al., 1998b; Lazetic et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NKG2B is a spliced form of NKG2A.
source: NKG2A and -B (a spliced form of –A) are inhibitory whereas NKG2C and -E are activating NK receptors (Kaiser et al., 2005; Braud et al., 1998b; Lazetic et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Both NKG2A and NKG2C are evolving under positive selection in primates.
source: An evolutionary analysis across primates revealed that both NKG2A and NKG2C are evolving under positive selection, suggesting that both genes have been actively engaged in host-pathogen conflict throughout primate evolution (Kaiser et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Engagement of peptide HLA-E/Qa-1 complex with CD94/NKG2 receptors in normal circumstances is believed to dominantly maintain self-tolerance and to sense aberrancy in MHC-I production.
source: Thus, engagement of peptide HLA-E/Qa-1 complex with CD94/NKG2 receptors in normal circumstances is believed to dominantly maintain self-tolerance and to sense aberrancy in MHC-I production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the established knowledge about CD94/NKG2 receptor function.

claim: RHVP was isolated from a lung homogenate of a pygmy rice rat caught in Peru.
source: Opportunities to address this issue have come from the identification of rodent herpesvirus Peru (RHVP) that was isolated from a lung homogenate of a pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys microtis) caught in Peru (Loh et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: RHVP is a member of the rhadinovirus genus of γ−herpesviruses along with KSHV and γHV68.
source: RHVP is a member of the rhadinovirus genus of γ−herpesviruses along with KSHV and γHV68.
evidence: This is established taxonomic classification.

claim: RHVP can establish latent infection in normal B6 and 129 mice.
source: RHVP can establish latent infection in normal B6 and 129 mice, suggesting immune evasion mechanisms are utilized by the virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to the original RHVP isolation paper.

claim: RHVP encodes several unique ORFs that are not present in other γ−herpesviruses and appear to have immune evasion functions.
source: Indeed, RHVP encodes several unique ORFs that are not present in other γ−herpesviruses and appear to have immune evasion functions (Lubman et al., 2014; Lubman and Fremont, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The R12 protein encoded by RHVP (pK3) is a MARCH family E3 ubiquitin ligase that induces rapid degradation of MHC-I by direct interaction with the heavy chain transmembrane region in the ER.
source: We previously reported that the R12 protein encoded by RHVP, termed pK3 because of its similarities to the K3 proteins of KSHV and γHV68, is a MARCH (membrane-associated RING-CH) family E3 ubiquitin ligase that induces rapid degradation of MHC-I by direct interaction with the heavy chain transmembrane (TM) region in the ER (Herr et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: pK3 secondarily induces profound loss of the MHC-I-dedicated chaperone tapasin as well as TAP.
source: In addition, pK3 secondarily induces profound loss of the MHC-I-dedicated chaperone tapasin as well as TAP.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The 5' end of the RHVP genome contains a cluster of three previously annotated ORFs (R3, R2 and R1) with high similarity to MHC-I α1, α2 and α3 domains, respectively.
source: With this in mind, we were intrigued to find that the 5' end of the RHVP genome (1383 to 236 nucleotides in reverse direction) contains a cluster of three previously annotated ORFs (R3, R2 and R1) with high similarity to MHC-I α1, α2 and α3 domains, respectively (Loh et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original RHVP genome annotation.

claim: Two putative introns that flank consensus splicing donor/acceptor sites were detected in between the putative α1 and α2, as well as the α2 and α3 coding sequences of pQa-1.
source: More strikingly, two putative introns that flank consensus splicing donor/acceptor sites (Keller and Noon, 1984) were detected in between the putative α1 and α2, as well as the α2 and α3 coding sequences (Figure 1A, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and reference to consensus splicing sites, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The sequences amplified by PCR from the cDNA pool using primers to the 5' end of R3 and 3' end of R1 was consistent with predicted splicing events.
source: The sequences amplified by PCR from the cDNA pool using a forward primer to the 5' end of R3 and a reverse primer to the 3' end of R1 was consistent with predicted splicing events (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–1A and S1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the splicing events of pQa-1, two introns containing 88 and 82 nucleotides, respectively, were excised.
source: In these splicing events, the two introns containing 88 and 82 nucleotides, respectively, were excised (Figure 1A, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The organization of exons and introns in pQa-1 is analogous to mammalian MHC-I genes as exemplified by the mouse Qa-1 gene.
source: This organization of exons and introns is analogous to mammalian MHC-I genes as exemplified by the mouse Qa-1 gene (Figure 1A, lower panel), suggesting that this ORF (here annotated as pQa-1) originated as a horizontal transfer from the host to the virus.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison shown in Figure 1A.

claim: pQa-1 originated as a horizontal transfer from the host to the virus.
source: This organization of exons and introns is analogous to mammalian MHC-I genes as exemplified by the mouse Qa-1 gene (Figure 1A, lower panel), suggesting that this ORF (here annotated as pQa-1) originated as a horizontal transfer from the host to the virus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of gene structure to host genes.

claim: pK3 coding sequence was concurrently amplified from the cDNA pool using primers specific to the ORF of pK3.
source: Notably, the pK3 coding sequence was also concurrently amplified from the cDNA pool using primers specific to the ORF of pK3, suggesting the two proteins are co-expressed within 24 hr post-infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1–1C.

claim: pK3 and pQa-1 are co-expressed within 24 hr post-infection.
source: Notably, the pK3 coding sequence was also concurrently amplified from the cDNA pool using primers specific to the ORF of pK3, suggesting the two proteins are co-expressed within 24 hr post-infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the concurrent detection of both transcripts in infected cells.

claim: The putative mature viral protein after signal peptide cleavage (residues 1–280 corresponding to the α1–3 ectodomains) yielded strong similarity to Qa-1 proteins (>56% identity) from mouse, rat, hamster and vole.
source: Sequence comparisons using the putative mature viral protein after signal peptide cleavage (residues 1–280 corresponding to the α1–3 ectodomains) yielded strong similarity to Qa-1 proteins (>56% identity) from mouse, rat, hamster and vole and slightly less strong similarity to some classical MHC-I proteins from human, monkey, panda, wild boar and harbor seal (54–52% identity) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence comparison data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis revealed that pQa-1 shares more similarity with rat and mouse Qa-1 than human HLA-E or mouse/human classical MHC-I.
source: Furthermore, phylogenetic analysis revealed that this viral MHC-I-like protein shares more similarity with rat and mouse Qa-1 than human HLA-E or mouse/human classical MHC-I (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 1B.

claim: pQa-1 contains substitutions of Ser and Leu at the Thr143 and Trp147 residues that contribute to peptide binding in the F pocket of classical MHC-I.
source: Similar to Qa-1, it contains substitutions of Ser and Leu at the Thr143 and Trp147 residues that contribute to peptide binding in the F pocket of classical MHC-I (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2.

claim: pQa-1 was not predicted to have a canonical TM region or a C-terminal cytoplasmic tail.
source: However, it should be noted that distinct from Qa-1, pQa-1 was not predicted to have a canonical TM region or a C-terminal cytoplasmic tail.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of pQa-1.

claim: pQa-1 was predicted by GPI-SOM to potentially be GPI anchored at residue 290.
source: Instead, it was predicted by GPI-SOM (Fankhauser and Mäser, 2005) to potentially be GPI anchored at residue 290 (Figure 1A, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction using GPI-SOM software.

claim: Low levels of surface pQa-1 in mouse and human cells were detected by flow cytometry using an anti-HA antibody.
source: Low levels of surface pQa-1 in mouse and human cells were detected by flow cytometry using an anti-HA antibody (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The low level expression of viral pQa-1 is similar to what has been reported for mouse Qa-1.
source: This low level expression of viral pQa-1 is similar to what has been reported for mouse Qa-1 (Gays et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Surface levels of pQa-1 and Ld-pQa-1 but not wild type Ld were both reduced upon a low dose GPI-cleaving enzyme PI-PLC treatment.
source: Surface levels of pQa-1 and Ld-pQa-1 but not wild type Ld were both reduced upon a low dose GPI-cleaving enzyme phosphatidylinositol-specific phospholipase C (PI-PLC) treatment, indicating that both proteins were cell surface tethered via GPI anchors (Figure 2C, left panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data after PI-PLC treatment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The sensitivity of Ld-pQa-1 to PI-PLC treatment was dose dependent.
source: The sensitivity of Ld-pQa-1 to PI-PLC treatment was dose dependent and the extent of reduction in fluorescence signal upon treatment with different doses of PI-PLC is similar to that of a known GPI-anchored protein, Thy1.1, expressed on the same cells (Figure 2C, right panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: pQa-1 was associated with β2-microblobulin (β2m).
source: Further, we found that pQa-1 was associated with β2-microblobulin (β2m) by labeling pQa-1-expressing cells with [35S] Cys/Met followed by immunoprecipitation of pQa-1, or by immunoprecipitation of pQa-1 followed by western blot of β2m (Figure 2D, left and right panel, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Without β2m in a H2-Kb-/-, H2-Db-/- and Β2m-/- MEF line (designated 3KO) pQa-1 was barely detected.
source: In addition, we found that without β2m in a H2-Kb-/-, H2-Db-/- and Β2m-/- MEF line (designated 3KO) pQa-1 was barely detected, while reconstitution of β2m into 3KO cells by retroviral transduction clearly enhanced surface expression of pQa-1 (Figure 2E), indicating that endogenous β2m is required for surface expression of pQa-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Endogenous β2m is required for surface expression of pQa-1.
source: In addition, we found that without β2m in a H2-Kb-/-, H2-Db-/- and Β2m-/- MEF line (designated 3KO) pQa-1 was barely detected, while reconstitution of β2m into 3KO cells by retroviral transduction clearly enhanced surface expression of pQa-1 (Figure 2E), indicating that endogenous β2m is required for surface expression of pQa-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that pQa-1 expression is enhanced by β2m reconstitution.

claim: Qa-1 preferentially binds the peptide AMAPRTLLL (Qdm) derived from the leader sequence of H2-D or H2-L in a TAP-dependent manner.
source: One of the hallmarks of Qa-1 is its propensity to preferentially bind the peptide AMAPRTLLL (also called Qa-1 determinant modifier or Qdm) derived from the leader sequence of H2-D or H2-L in a TAP-dependent manner (DeCloux et al., 1997; Bai et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NK cytotoxicity can be inhibited by the engagement of CD94/NKG2A with its ligand Qa-1 and this inhibitory effect is highly dependent on Qa-1 being loaded with the Qdm peptide.
source: NK cytotoxicity can be inhibited by the engagement of CD94/NKG2A with its ligand Qa-1 and this inhibitory effect is highly dependent on Qa-1 being loaded with the Qdm peptide (Kraft et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A modest but significant enhancement in pQa-1 levels was observed when co-cultured with Qdm but not the OVA peptide at 37°C for 4 hr.
source: A modest but significant enhancement in pQa-1 levels was observed when co-cultured with Qdm but not the OVA peptide at 37°C for 4 hr, although the OVA peptide enhanced the level of surface Kb on the same cells as reported (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Surface levels of pQa-1 were significantly enhanced when cells were cultured at 27°C for 4 hr with Qdm or with the Qdm-like nonamers that have one residue difference at the P1, P2 or P3 position compared to no peptide added.
source: Surface levels of pQa-1 were significantly enhanced when cells were cultured at 27°C for 4 hr with Qdm or with the Qdm-like nonamers that have one residue difference at the P1, P2 or P3 position compared to no peptide added (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An octameric peptide that lacks the P1 residue of Qdm did not increase surface pQa-1.
source: In contrast to the nonamers, an octameric peptide that lacks the P1 residue of Qdm did not increase surface pQa-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the peptide-binding assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: pQa-1 prefers to bind a Qdm-like nonamer and tolerates certain variations in peptide sequence.
source: This analysis suggests that pQa-1 prefers to bind a Qdm-like nonamer and tolerates certain variations in peptide sequence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the peptide-binding assay results.

claim: Single substitution with G/A at P1 and P3 or K at P1 in Qdm did not appear to impact peptide binding to mouse Qa-1.
source: This is very similar to the observations made with mouse Qa-1 where single substitution with G/A at P1 and P3 or K at P1 in Qdm did not appear to impact peptide binding (Kurepa and Forman, 1997; Kraft et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Surface pQa-1 in stably transduced cells increased after IFNγ treatment.
source: It is noteworthy that surface pQa-1 in stably transduced cells increased after IFNγ treatment (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TAP1-deficient fibroblasts stably transduced with pQa-1 express a low level on the cell surface, and this level can be enhanced by IFNγ treatment.
source: We found, similar to what we had observed with wildtype MEF cells, that TAP1-deficient fibroblasts stably transduced with pQa-1 express a low level on the cell surface, and this level can be enhanced by IFNγ treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of pQa-1 on TAP-deficient cells suggests pQa-1 can load peptide independently of TAP as has been seen for Qa-1 and HLA-E.
source: Thus, expression of pQa-1 on TAP-deficient cells suggests pQa-1 can load peptide independently of TAP as has been seen for Qa-1 and HLA-E (Lampen et al., 2013; Oliveira et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of pQa-1 expression in TAP-deficient cells, supported by citations to similar findings for Qa-1 and HLA-E.

claim: pK3 efficiently downregulates surface MHC-I by targeting newly synthesized MHC-I in the ER for rapid, ubiquitination-mediated degradation (ERAD).
source: We previously demonstrated that pK3, a MARCH family E3 ligase encoded by RHVP, efficiently downregulates surface MHC-I by targeting newly synthesized MHC-I in the ER for rapid, ubiquitination-mediated degradation (so called ER-associated degradation, ERAD) (Herr et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: pK3 targets MHC-I through direct interaction with the TM region of MHC-I proteins.
source: In contrast to mK3 of γHV68 that directly interacts with TAP to capture TAP-associated MHC-I, pK3 targets MHC-I through direct interaction with the TM region of MHC-I proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: In the presence of pK3 WT, Qa-1 was significantly down regulated, like classical MHC-I.
source: Indeed, in the presence of pK3 WT, Qa-1 was significantly down regulated, like classical MHC-I, even though Qa-1 was not as well expressed as pQa-1 in these experiments (Figure 4A, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Downregulation of Qa-1 by pK3 was more evident with higher baseline expression of endogenous Qa-1 in RMA cells.
source: Downregulation of Qa-1 by pK3 was more evident with higher baseline expression of endogenous Qa-1 in RMA cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Surface pQa-1 remained unchanged in the presence of pK3.
source: In contrast, surface pQa-1 remained unchanged in the presence of pK3 (Figure 4A, upper panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Downregulation of MHC-I and Qa-1 was not observed in the presence of the catalytically inactive pK3 RM, demonstrating that E3 ubiquitin ligase activity was required.
source: Importantly, downregulation of MHC-I and Qa-1 was not observed in the presence of the catalytically inactive pK3 RM, demonstrating that E3 ubiquitin ligase activity was required.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing pK3 WT and pK3 RM effects.

claim: The GPI anchored classical MHC-I chimera, Ld-pQa-1, was resistant to pK3.
source: In addition, the GPI anchored classical MHC-I chimera, Ld-pQa-1, was resistant to pK3, whereas the reciprocal chimera with α1-α2 domains of pQa-1 and α3-TM-cytoplasmic tail of Ld (pQa-1-Ld) remained as sensitive to pK3 as wild type Ld (Figure 4C), supporting the conclusion that pQa-1 resistance to pK3 is associated with its unique C-terminal tail.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The reciprocal chimera pQa-1-Ld remained as sensitive to pK3 as wild type Ld.
source: In addition, the GPI anchored classical MHC-I chimera, Ld-pQa-1, was resistant to pK3, whereas the reciprocal chimera with α1-α2 domains of pQa-1 and α3-TM-cytoplasmic tail of Ld (pQa-1-Ld) remained as sensitive to pK3 as wild type Ld (Figure 4C), supporting the conclusion that pQa-1 resistance to pK3 is associated with its unique C-terminal tail.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: pQa-1 resistance to pK3 is associated with its unique C-terminal tail.
source: In addition, the GPI anchored classical MHC-I chimera, Ld-pQa-1, was resistant to pK3, whereas the reciprocal chimera with α1-α2 domains of pQa-1 and α3-TM-cytoplasmic tail of Ld (pQa-1-Ld) remained as sensitive to pK3 as wild type Ld (Figure 4C), supporting the conclusion that pQa-1 resistance to pK3 is associated with its unique C-terminal tail.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential sensitivity of chimeric constructs to pK3.

claim: pQa-1-SCT appeared to be more stable than pQa-1.
source: As we previously observed with classical MHC-I (Mitaksov et al., 2007; Truscott et al., 2007), the pQa-1-SCT appeared to be more stable than pQa-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to previous observations with classical MHC-I SCTs and thermostability data.

claim: The surface levels of GPI anchored pQa-1-SCT and pQa-1-dtSCT were 6–8 folds higher than pQa-1 expressed alone.
source: The surface levels of GPI anchored pQa-1-SCT and pQa-1-dtSCT were 6–8 folds higher than pQa-1 expressed alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 5–1A); and their thermostabilities as measured by circular dichroism melting analysis were comparable to those reported for classical MHC-I Kb-SCT (Figure 5—figure supplement 5–1B and Mitaksov et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5–1A.

claim: The thermostabilities of pQa-1-SCT and pQa-1-dtSCT as measured by circular dichroism melting analysis were comparable to those reported for classical MHC-I Kb-SCT.
source: The surface levels of GPI anchored pQa-1-SCT and pQa-1-dtSCT were 6–8 folds higher than pQa-1 expressed alone (Figure 5—figure supplement 5–1A); and their thermostabilities as measured by circular dichroism melting analysis were comparable to those reported for classical MHC-I Kb-SCT (Figure 5—figure supplement 5–1B and Mitaksov et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by circular dichroism data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5–1B and comparison to published data.

claim: pQa-1-dtSCT tetramers stained the same population recognized by the NKG2A/C/E antibody.
source: These pQa-1-dtSCT tetramers stained the same population recognized by the NKG2A/C/E antibody (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The population stained by pQa-1-dtSCT tetramers consisted of about 40% of NK cells and 2% of CD8+ T cells in the splenocytes isolated from wildtype C57BL/6 mice.
source: This population consisted of about 40% of NK cells and 2% of CD8+ T cells in the splenocytes isolated from wildtype C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The median fluorescence intensity (MFI) of tetramer+ CD8+ cells was lower than NK cells.
source: Also similar to the level of anti-NKG2A/C/E antibody staining, the median fluorescence intensity (MFI) of tetramer+ CD8+ cells was lower than NK cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: NK and CD8+ cells from NKG2A-/- mice were not stained by pQa-1-dtSCT tetramer or the NKG2A/C/E antibody.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to the wildtype mice, NK and CD8+ cells from NKG2A-/- mice were not stained by pQa-1-dtSCT tetramer or the NKG2A/C/E antibody (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: pQa-1 is able to selectively engage CD94/NKG2 receptors on murine cytotoxic cells.
source: Thus, pQa-1 is able to selectively engage CD94/NKG2 receptors on murine cytotoxic cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tetramer staining data.

claim: When cultured with CHO-pQa-1 cells in the presence of Qdm or Qdm-k peptide, but not a peptide that cannot stabilize surface pQa-1, mouse spleen NKG2A+ NK cells showed less IFNγ production than NKG2A- cells.
source: When cultured with CHO-pQa-1 cells in the presence of Qdm or Qdm-k peptide, but not a peptide that cannot stabilize surface pQa-1, mouse spleen NKG2A+ NK cells showed less IFNγ production than NKG2A- cells, which was not the case upon culture with control CHO-V cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: A similar decrease in IFNγ production was observed when NK cells were incubated with CHO cells expressing the natural NKG2A ligand Qa-1.
source: A similar decrease in IFNγ production was observed when NK cells were incubated with CHO cells expressing the natural NKG2A ligand Qa-1 (Figure 6A and B), suggesting that an inhibitory effect comparable to mouse Qa-1 on NK activity was mediated by the expression of viral pQa-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: The suppressive effect of pQa-1 on NK cells could be reversed by the NKG2A/C/E blocking antibodies but not by an isotype control.
source: In addition, like Qa-1, this suppressive effect could be reversed by the NKG2A/C/E blocking antibodies but not by an isotype control, demonstrating that pQa-1 exerts its effect specifically through the NKG2A receptor (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CHO cells expressing pQa-1-SCT showed significantly stronger suppression on NKG2A+ NK cells in IFNγ production as well as CD107a expression compared with CHO-pQa-1 or CHO-Qa-1 cells.
source: Furthermore, compared with the inhibitory effect mediated by CHO-pQa-1 or CHO-Qa-1 cells, CHO cells expressing pQa-1-SCT showed significantly stronger suppression on NKG2A+ NK cells in IFNγ production as well as CD107a expression, which again could be blocked by the NKG2A/C/E-specific antibody (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Increased NKG2A+ NK cell activation was observed when CHO-pQa-1-SCT was cleaved off the cell surface by PI-PLC treatment.
source: We observed increased NKG2A+ NK cell activation, as measured by IFNγ production and CD107a degranulation, when CHO-pQa-1-SCT was cleaved off the cell surface (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 6–1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: pQa-1 can functionally mimic Qa-1 to mediate inhibition of NK cells by specific engagement of the inhibitory receptor CD94/NKG2A.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that pQa-1 can functionally mimic Qa-1 to mediate inhibition of NK cells by specific engagement of the inhibitory receptor CD94/NKG2A.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NK activation assay results.

claim: HLA-E/Qa-1 can activate HLA-E/Qa-1 restricted CD8+ T cells by presenting pathogen-derived or unconventional self-peptides.
source: Recent reports suggest that HLA-E/Qa-1 can activate HLA-E/Qa-1 restricted CD8+ T cells by presenting pathogen-derived or unconventional self-peptides (Hansen et al., 2016; Bian et al., 2017; Oliveira et al., 2010), which likely occurs when canonical MHC-I antigen presentation is impaired (Oliveira et al., 2010; Nagarajan et al., 2012; Lampen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Co-culturing T2-Qa-1 cells with Ln12 cells resulted in significant IFNγ production in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Co-culturing T2-Qa-1 cells, the TAP-deficient cell line transduced to express Qa-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 6–1B) with Ln12 cells resulted in significant IFNγ production in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Using T2 cells expressing pQa-1, no T-cell activation was observed when co-cultured with Ln12 cells.
source: However, under the same conditions, using T2 cells expressing pQa-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 6–1B) we observed no T-cell activation (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Viral pQa-1 may not conserve antigen presentation properties with Qa-1.
source: Thus, it appears that in contrast to its mimicry of Qa-1 in CD94/NKG2A interactions, viral pQa-1 may not conserve antigen presentation properties with Qa-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of T-cell activation by pQa-1-expressing cells.

claim: Challenge of C57BL/6 mice with B16F10-pQa-1-dtSCT cells resulted in at least two-fold more lung metastases compared to mice challenged with B16F10 cells expressing empty vector.
source: Consistent with the inhibitory effect of pQa-1 on NK cell activation in vitro, challenge of C57BL/6 mice with B16F10-pQa-1-dtSCT cells resulted in at least two-fold more lung metastases compared to mice challenged with B16F10 cells expressing empty vector (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo metastasis data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: pQa-1 has the capacity to protect cells from NK control in vivo.
source: These data thus demonstrate that pQa-1 has the capacity to protect cells from NK control in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vivo metastasis data.

claim: A significantly higher percentage of cells expressing pK3 were killed than cells expressing the pK3 RING mutant when cultured with syngeneic NK cells from mouse spleen.
source: When cultured with syngeneic NK cells from mouse spleen, a significantly higher percentage of cells expressing pK3 were killed than cells expressing the pK3 RING mutant, demonstrating that a decrease of surface MHC-I induced by pK3 rendered cells susceptible to NK killing (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by NK cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cells co-expressing pQa-1 with pK3 showed reduced susceptibility to NK cell killing compared to cells expressing only pK3.
source: Moreover, in comparison to cells expressing only pK3, cells co-expressing pQa-1 with pK3 showed reduced susceptibility to NK cell killing.
evidence: This claim is supported by NK cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The reduction in NK killing by pQa-1 co-expression was not evident when NK cells from NKG2A-/- mice were used.
source: This reduction was not evident when NK cells from NKG2A-/- mice were used, indicating the protection provided by expression of pQa-1 is mediated by engagement of CD94/NKG2A (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by NK cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A small decrease in pQa-1 surface expression on target cells after PI-PLC treatment was found to correlate with a modest increase in NK killing.
source: Consistently, a small decrease in pQa-1 surface expression on target cells after PI-PLC treatment was found to correlate with a modest increase in NK killing (Figure 7—figure supplement 7–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by NK cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 7–2.

claim: Resistance of pQa-1 to pK3 is functionally important.
source: Together these data indicate that resistance of pQa-1 to pK3 is functionally important and suggest that RHVP has evolved a mechanism for thwarting 'missing self' recognition by NK cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NK cytotoxicity assay results.

claim: RHVP has evolved a mechanism for thwarting 'missing self' recognition by NK cells.
source: Together these data indicate that resistance of pQa-1 to pK3 is functionally important and suggest that RHVP has evolved a mechanism for thwarting 'missing self' recognition by NK cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined findings about pK3 and pQa-1.

claim: A viral mimic of Qa-1 has not been previously noted.
source: Although manipulation of host HLA-E/Qa-1 surface expression has been reported as a NK evasion strategy by other viruses, a viral mimic of Qa-1 has not been previously noted.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding based on literature review.

claim: The pQa-1 ORF is unusual in that the mRNA is produced by splicing of a primary transcript with an exon structure analogous to that found in mammalian MHC-I.
source: The pQa-1 ORF is unusual in that the mRNA is produced by splicing of a primary transcript with an exon structure analogous to that found in mammalian MHC-I.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-PCR and sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The putative α1–3 domains of pQa-1 have >56% sequence identity to mouse and rat Qa-1.
source: The putative α1–3 domains of pQa-1 have >56% sequence identity to mouse and rat Qa-1, and it conserves the functional characteristics of Qa-1 including association with β2m and low level cell surface expression stabilized by Qdm or Qdm-like peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence comparison data.

claim: pQa-1 conserves the functional characteristics of Qa-1 including association with β2m and low level cell surface expression stabilized by Qdm or Qdm-like peptides.
source: The putative α1–3 domains of pQa-1 have >56% sequence identity to mouse and rat Qa-1, and it conserves the functional characteristics of Qa-1 including association with β2m and low level cell surface expression stabilized by Qdm or Qdm-like peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: pQa-1 mimics Qa-1 function by effectively engaging the inhibitory NK receptor CD94/NKG2A.
source: More impressively, pQa-1 mimics Qa-1 function by effectively engaging the inhibitory NK receptor CD94/NKG2A, yet is resistant to downregulation by the RHVP encoded MHC-I subversion protein pK3.
evidence: This claim is supported by the tetramer staining and NK activation assay data.

claim: Expression of pQa-1 inhibits NK activation in vitro.
source: Expression of pQa-1 inhibits NK activation in vitro and protects tumor cells from NK control in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by the NK activation assay data.

claim: pK3-induced loss of surface MHC-I renders cells susceptible to syngeneic NK killing.
source: In addition, we demonstrate that pK3-induced loss of surface MHC-I renders cells susceptible to syngeneic NK killing, whereas concomitant co-expression of pQa-1 reduces cell susceptibility to NK killing in a NKG2A-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by the NK cytotoxicity assay data.

claim: Concomitant co-expression of pQa-1 reduces cell susceptibility to NK killing in a NKG2A-dependent manner.
source: In addition, we demonstrate that pK3-induced loss of surface MHC-I renders cells susceptible to syngeneic NK killing, whereas concomitant co-expression of pQa-1 reduces cell susceptibility to NK killing in a NKG2A-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by the NK cytotoxicity assay data.

claim: RHVP employs compensatory mechanisms to concurrently sabotage CTL and NK-mediated immunity.
source: Thus, our findings demonstrate that RHVP employs compensatory mechanisms to concurrently sabotage CTL and NK-mediated immunity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined findings about pK3 and pQa-1.

claim: The ability of herpesviruses to utilize RNA splicing as a means to expand their coding capacity was not appreciated until recently.
source: The ability of herpesviruses to utilize RNA splicing as a means to expand their coding capacity was not appreciated until recently (Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012; Conrad, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Through mRNA-sequencing, up to 27 splicing junctions, corresponding to one or more introns in 17 viral genes (20% of genes) of KSHV were identified and seven of them were previously unrecognized.
source: For example, through mRNA-sequencing, up to 27 splicing junctions, corresponding to one or more introns in 17 viral genes (20% of genes) of KSHV were identified and seven of them were previously unrecognized (Arias et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The observation of spliced messenger RNA from RHVP is similar to what has been observed in KSHV.
source: Our observation of spliced messenger RNA from RHVP is similar to what has been observed in KSHV, suggesting that the actual coding capacity and protein repertoire of γ−herpesviruses is likely larger and more elaborate than was previously appreciated.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to KSHV findings.

claim: The actual coding capacity and protein repertoire of γ−herpesviruses is likely larger and more elaborate than was previously appreciated.
source: Our observation of spliced messenger RNA from RHVP is similar to what has been observed in KSHV, suggesting that the actual coding capacity and protein repertoire of γ−herpesviruses is likely larger and more elaborate than was previously appreciated.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings about RNA splicing in RHVP and KSHV.

claim: The high degree of similarity in both sequence and function between pQa-1 and Qa-1 along with the conservation of the intron splicing sites suggest that the coding sequence of pQa-1 was acquired by horizontal transfer.
source: The high degree of similarity in both sequence and function between pQa-1 and Qa-1 along with the conservation of the intron splicing sites suggest that the coding sequence of pQa-1 was acquired by horizontal transfer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence and structural similarities.

claim: Viral MHC-I-like proteins such as members of the m145 family of MCMV and UL18 of HCMV possess a common MHC-I fold but are highly divergent in amino acid sequence (≤25% identity).
source: Those viral MHC-I-like proteins, such as members of the m145 family of MCMV and UL18 of HCMV, possess a common MHC-I fold but are highly divergent in amino acid sequence (≤25% identity).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The mRNA transcripts of viral MHC-I-like proteins such as m145 family and UL18 are not spliced.
source: In addition, their mRNA transcripts are not spliced, suggesting they may have been acquired from host transcripts as has been shown in other dsDNA viruses (Grossegesse et al., 2017; Greijer et al., 2000; Bresnahan and Shenk, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Replacement of canonical TM and cytoplasmic tail with GPI anchor appears to be an adaptive modification to avoid harmful recognition events in both pathogens and hosts.
source: Thus, replacement of canonical TM and cytoplasmic tail with GPI anchor appears to be an adaptive modification to avoid harmful recognition events in both pathogens and hosts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations about pQa-1 and MICA*008.

claim: MICA*008 is the most frequently expressed allele of MICA in diverse populations worldwide.
source: For example, distinct from other alleles that possess a TM and a cytoplasmic tail, MICA*008, the most frequently expressed allele of MICA in diverse populations worldwide, is GPI-anchored which is associated with its resistance to kK5, a MARCH ubiquitin E3 ligase similar to the pK3 encoded by KSHV.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MICA*008 is GPI-anchored which is associated with its resistance to kK5.
source: For example, distinct from other alleles that possess a TM and a cytoplasmic tail, MICA*008, the most frequently expressed allele of MICA in diverse populations worldwide, is GPI-anchored which is associated with its resistance to kK5, a MARCH ubiquitin E3 ligase similar to the pK3 encoded by KSHV.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: kK5-mediated downregulation of MICA requires lysine residues in the cytoplasmic tail of MICA for ubiquitination and subsequent internalization.
source: kK5-mediated downregulation of MICA requires lysine residues in the cytoplasmic tail of MICA for ubiquitination and subsequent internalization (Thomas et al., 2008; Ashiru et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most γ−herpesviruses in the genus rhadinovirus employ less complex strategies to avoid attack by CTL compared to β−herpesviruses.
source: Compared to β−herpesviruses in which multiple proteins function to evade CTL and NK detection, most γ−herpesviruses in the genus rhadinovirus employ less complex strategies to avoid attack by CTL, and their NK evasion mechanisms are not well understood.
evidence: This is a general statement based on knowledge of herpesvirus immune evasion strategies.

claim: A major CTL evasion mechanism in rhadinoviruses is carried out by a group of MARCH family ubiquitin ligases.
source: A major CTL evasion mechanism in rhadinoviruses is carried out by a group of MARCH family ubiquitin ligases (Hansen and Bouvier, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: kK5 and kK3 of KSHV target mature MHC-I by conjugating a K63-linked ubiquitin chain on the tail of mature MHC-I heavy chain, which results in rapid endocytosis of MHC-I complex followed by its degradation in the lysosome.
source: For example, kK5 and kK3 of KSHV target mature MHC-I by conjugating a K63-linked ubiquitin chain on the tail of mature MHC-I heavy chain, which results in rapid endocytosis of MHC-I complex followed by its degradation in the lysosome (Duncan et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: mK3 of γHV68 acts at an earlier point in MHC class I biosynthesis.
source: In contrast, mK3 of γHV68 acts at an earlier point in MHC class I biosynthesis (Boname and Stevenson, 2001; Yu et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: mK3 of γHV68 targets TAP-associated MHC-I in the ER by direct interaction with TAP, which results in K48-linked ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of MHC-I by the proteasome.
source: It targets TAP-associated MHC-I in the ER by direct interaction with TAP, which results in K48-linked ubiquitination and subsequent degradation of MHC-I by the proteasome.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: pK3 of RHVP not only induces dramatic loss of MHC-I but also TAP and tapasin.
source: Functionally, pK3 not only induces dramatic loss of MHC-I but also TAP and tapasin (Herr et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: KSHV, γHV68 and RHVP appear to have divergent strategies to avoid NK attack.
source: As compared to the molecular mechanisms involved in MHC-I downregulation by the viral MARCH E3 ligases, KSHV, γHV68 and RHVP appear to have divergent strategies to avoid NK attack.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of NK evasion strategies.

claim: kK5 downregulates MICA and MICB, the ligands of conserved activating NK receptor NKG2D, to evade NK cell cytotoxicity.
source: For example, other than selectively targeting MHC-I to maintain expression of HLA-E, kK5 also downregulates MICA and MICB, the ligands of conserved activating NK receptor NKG2D, to evade NK cell cytotoxicity (Thomas et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: KSHV produces a miRNA that targets MICB at the transcriptional level.
source: In addition, KSHV produces a miRNA that targets MICB at the transcriptional level (Nachmani et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The target spectrum of mK3 is limited and it binds primarily TAP and only targets MHC-I heavy chains that are associated with TAP/tapasin complex.
source: In contrast to kK3 and kK5, the target spectrum of mK3 is limited. It binds primarily TAP and only targets MHC-I heavy chains that are associated with TAP/tapasin complex (Lybarger et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: There have been no MHC-I-like proteins or NK inhibitory mechanisms identified in the genome of γHV68 thus far.
source: There have been no MHC-I-like proteins or NK inhibitory mechanisms identified in the genome of γHV68 thus far.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: NK evasion strategies in γ−herpesviruses evolve with selection pressure imposed by CTL evasion and are intimately linked to the CTL subversion mechanisms employed by the virus.
source: Collectively these observations support the hypothesis that NK evasion strategies in γ−herpesviruses evolve with selection pressure imposed by CTL evasion and are intimately linked to the CTL subversion mechanisms employed by the virus.
evidence: This is speculation based on the comparative analysis of different herpesvirus strategies.

claim: HLA-E/Qa-1 has been reported to play a role in adaptive immunity against intracellular pathogens or tumors by presenting microbial-derived peptides or self-peptides other than Qdm to HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8+ T cells.
source: In addition to its function in innate immunity, HLA-E/Qa-1 has been reported to play a role in adaptive immunity against intracellular pathogens or tumors by presenting microbial-derived peptides or self-peptides other than Qdm to HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8+ T cells (van Hall et al., 2010; Joosten et al., 2016; Kraemer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The acidic alpha-3 domain CD loop critical for interaction with CD8 and shared by classical MHC-I and Qa-1 is not conserved in pQa-1.
source: Further, the acidic alpha-3 domain CD loop (Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2) critical for interaction with CD8 (Connolly et al., 1990; Chang et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2009) and shared by classical MHC-I and Qa-1 is not conserved in pQa-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1–2 and citations to published literature.
